name: Data Structures and Algorithms
audience: Developers preparing for technical interviews or wanting a solid algorithms foundation, using Python. Basic Python assumed.
format: This site's course with a 40-question practice test of complexity analysis, trace-the-algorithm, choose-the-structure and debugging questions.
scenarios: A coding interview at a large tech company
Choosing a data structure for a cache
Ranking and top-k over a stream
verifyNotes: This is the site's own deep-foundations course, not a vendor certification: there are no exam facts to confirm, so spend Research on finding the best official/primary sources per topic (URLs that will be cited as sources). Goal: the learner can explain and reason about every idea confidently in a senior interview or design review. Lessons go deep: intuition first, then the precise definition or mechanism, then a fully worked example, then where it matters in real systems (including AI/ML and LLM application code where natural), then a common misconception. Write math in LaTeX between double dollars only: $$...$$; NEVER single-dollar math (single $ renders literally). In JSON strings escape backslashes (\\log). Code in fenced ```python blocks that run as-is. Every lesson has a hands-on lab: a small Python exercise with the expected output. Verifiers MUST run every compute and code-output question with {{root}}/.pipeline/py313/bin/python (CPython 3.13, standard library only) and fix keys that disagree; state any randomness seed in the stem; never depend on dict/set ordering that Python does not guarantee, or on id() values. Question mix: ~35% concept/judgment (choose the structure or algorithm, state its complexity), ~40% trace or compute (run the algorithm by hand on given input, give the result or the cost), ~25% debug-or-choose-the-right-approach (off-by-one, wrong invariant, wrong base case). Every algorithm lesson states time and space complexity with a short justification, gives a correct runnable Python implementation, and includes a correctness argument (loop invariant, exchange argument or induction) at a working level. Use Python's own structures where they exist (list, dict, set, collections.deque, heapq, bisect) and explain their costs. Sources: MIT OpenCourseWare (6.006, 6.046), Princeton Algorithms (algs4.cs.princeton.edu), Stanford course pages, and docs.python.org (including the TimeComplexity wiki page on wiki.python.org) only; no blogs, Medium or LeetCode solution posts.

domains.name: Complexity and algorithmic thinking
skills: Asymptotic notation: Big-O, Theta, Omega; best, worst and average case
Amortized analysis: dynamic array growth, aggregate and accounting arguments
Recursion and recurrences: recursion trees and the master theorem
Correctness: loop invariants, induction, and testing edge cases
Python's cost model: list, dict, set, deque and string operation costs

domains.name: Arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues and hashing
skills: Dynamic arrays and linked lists: operations, costs and when each wins
Stacks, queues, deques and monotonic stacks/queues
Hash tables: hashing, collisions (chaining, open addressing), load factor and resizing
Array techniques: two pointers, sliding window, prefix sums and difference arrays
Designing with hashing: frequency counts, deduplication, LRU cache (OrderedDict or hash map + linked list)

domains.name: Trees, heaps and advanced structures
skills: Binary trees: traversals (pre, in, post, level order), height and recursion on trees
Binary search trees and balanced trees (AVL and red-black at a conceptual level)
Heaps and priority queues: heapify, push/pop costs, top-k and k-way merge with heapq
Tries and prefix search
Union-find with path compression and union by rank; segment and Fenwick trees for range queries

domains.name: Sorting, searching and divide and conquer
skills: Comparison sorts: merge sort, quicksort, heapsort; stability; the Omega(n log n) lower bound
Non-comparison sorts: counting and radix sort; Python's Timsort and key functions
Binary search: invariants, lower/upper bound with bisect, searching on the answer
Divide and conquer and quickselect for order statistics
Choosing the right sort or search for the data

domains.name: Graphs
skills: Graph representations (adjacency list vs matrix) and modelling problems as graphs
BFS and DFS: shortest paths in unweighted graphs, connected components, cycle detection
Topological sort (Kahn and DFS) and dependency resolution
Weighted shortest paths: Dijkstra with a heap, Bellman-Ford and negative edges
Minimum spanning trees (Kruskal, Prim) and strongly connected components

domains.name: Dynamic programming, greedy and problem solving
skills: Dynamic programming: optimal substructure, memoization vs tabulation, state design
Classic DP: knapsack, longest increasing subsequence, edit distance, grid paths, interval DP
Greedy algorithms and exchange arguments: interval scheduling, Huffman coding
Backtracking: permutations, subsets, constraint search and pruning
Problem-solving method for interviews; P, NP and NP-completeness at a working level
